# 01 Roadmap for Backend from First Principles

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/02 Walk the Path of a True Backend Engineer/02 Walk the Path of a True Backend Engineer|02 Walk the Path of a True Backend Engineer]]

This lesson is a map of the whole series. It explains **why** the series exists and then walks through every topic it will cover, in order. Use this note as a checklist: when you finish a lesson, come back here and see where it fits in the big picture.

---

## 1. What backend engineering really is

A common beginner idea is that backend work means writing **CRUD APIs**.

- **CRUD** = **C**reate, **R**ead, **U**pdate, **D**elete — the four basic things you can do with stored data.
- **API** (Application Programming Interface) = a defined way for one program to talk to another. On the web, this is usually a set of URLs a client can send requests to.

CRUD APIs are only a small part of the job. Backend engineering is about building systems and codebases that are:

| Quality | What it means | Simple example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Reliable** | Works correctly, consistently | A payment is never charged twice |
| **Scalable** | Keeps working as users and data grow | Handles 10 users today and 1 million later |
| **Fault-tolerant** | Keeps going (or fails safely) when parts break | If the email service is down, signup still works |
| **Maintainable** | Easy for people to understand and change | A new teammate can add a feature without breaking others |
| **Efficient** | Doesn't waste time, memory, or money | Answers in 50 ms instead of 5 s |

## 2. Why learning backend is hard

### Problem 1: Too many scattered resources

There are thousands of tutorials, but no clear answer to:

- What should I learn first?
- How do these ideas connect?
- What does the big picture look like?

Most people start with a narrow course (college, bootcamp, or an online course) and fill the gaps over years through trial and error and help from other developers. The creator went through this too — reading many backend books and studying hundreds of open-source codebases — and built this series to shorten that path.

### Problem 2: Learning through one language or framework

Many people learn backend *through* a single framework, such as:

- **Express** (JavaScript / Node.js)
- **Spring Boot** (Java)
- **Ruby on Rails** (Ruby)

A **framework** is a ready-made structure of code that handles common tasks so you can focus on your app. The risk: you start seeing every problem through that one tool, and you have **blind spots** about what is actually happening underneath.

> **Example:** You have used Ruby on Rails for years. Your company decides to move to Go for better performance. If you only know "the Rails way", little of your knowledge transfers. If you understand the **underlying ideas** (HTTP, routing, validation, databases…), you can apply them in any language.

That is what "first principles" means here: learn the basic ideas that every backend shares, not just one tool's version of them.

---

## 3. The roadmap, topic by topic

The topics below are in the order they were presented. Where a topic has its own lesson in the playlist, it links to that note. Some roadmap items (such as the business logic layer and transactional emails) were described in the roadmap but are covered inside other lessons or not given their own video.

### 3.1 How a backend works at a high level

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/03 What Is a Backend/03 What Is a Backend|03 What Is a Backend]]

- How a request from your **browser** travels through several **hops** (intermediate machines), network **firewalls** (systems that filter traffic), and the Internet.
- How it reaches a backend **server** running on a remote machine (for example, on AWS — Amazon's cloud).
- How the server answers and what the **response** looks like.
- Goal: get a clear mental picture of how a **client** (the thing asking, like a browser) and a **server** (the thing answering) communicate.

### 3.2 HTTP

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers|05 HTTP for Backend Engineers]]

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules clients and servers use to exchange messages on the web. Planned subtopics:

- **Raw HTTP messages** — what a request and response actually look like as text.
- **Headers** — extra information attached to a message. Types mentioned: request headers, representation headers, general headers, and security headers.
- **Methods** — the "verb" of a request: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, when to use each, and the meaning (semantics) behind them.
- **CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) — how browsers decide whether a page from one site may call an API on another site. Includes **simple requests** vs **preflight requests** (an extra check the browser sends first). See also [[Notes/Web Development/CORS|CORS]].
- **Responses and status codes** — e.g. `200 OK`, `404 Not Found`; which to return when.
- **HTTP caching** — reusing earlier responses, using tools like **ETags** (a fingerprint of a response) and **max-age** (how long a response stays fresh).
- **HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3** — the versions and how they differ.
- **Content negotiation** — client and server agreeing on a format (e.g. JSON vs XML, language) using headers.
- **Persistent connections** — reusing one connection for many requests.
- **Compression** — shrinking responses with **gzip**, **deflate**, or **Brotli (br)**.
- **Security** — **SSL/TLS** (encryption) and **HTTPS** (HTTP over TLS).

### 3.3 Routing

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/06 Routing/06 Routing|06 Routing]]

**Routing** maps an incoming URL + HTTP method to the piece of server code that should handle it.

- **Path parameters** — values inside the path: `/users/42` → `id = 42`.
- **Query parameters** — values after `?`: `/users?page=2`.
- Route types: static, dynamic, nested, hierarchical, catch-all/wildcard, and regular-expression–based.
- **API versioning** — e.g. `/v1/users` vs `/v2/users`; different techniques, and how to **deprecate** (phase out) old versions properly.
- **Route grouping** — grouping routes so they share versioning, permissions, and middleware.
- Securing routes and making route matching fast.

### 3.4 Serialization and deserialization

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/07 Serialization and Deserialization/07 Serialization and Deserialization|07 Serialization and Deserialization]]

- **Serialization** = turning your program's in-memory data into a format that can be sent over the network (e.g. JSON text).
- **Deserialization** = turning received data back into your language's native structures (a Python dictionary, a Go struct, a JavaScript object).
- Why it matters: **interoperability** — programs in different languages can understand each other.

Planned subtopics:

- **Text formats** (JSON, XML) vs **binary formats** (Protocol Buffers / "protobuf").
- JSON structure and data types: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects; nested objects and collections.
- Common problems: missing or extra fields, `null` values, date formats, time zones.
- Custom serialization, and errors such as invalid data, conversion errors, unknown fields.
- Security: injection attacks; validating input (including with **JSON Schema**) *before* processing it.
- Performance: compression, dropping unnecessary fields.
- **Trade-off:** text formats are human-readable (you can inspect the payload easily); binary formats are faster and smaller but not readable. Choosing between them is a real design decision.

### 3.5 Authentication and authorization

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/08 Authentication and Authorization/08 Authentication and Authorization|08 Authentication and Authorization]]

- **Authentication** = *who are you?* (proving identity).
- **Authorization** = *what are you allowed to do?* (permissions).

Planned subtopics:

- **Stateful** vs **stateless** authentication (does the server remember you, or does each request carry proof?).
- Basic auth, bearer tokens, sessions, **JWTs** (JSON Web Tokens), cookies.
- **OAuth** and **OpenID Connect** (logging in through another service, like "Sign in with Google").
- API keys, **multi-factor authentication (MFA)**.
- **Hashing** and **salting** passwords and other cryptographic techniques.
- Access-control models: **ABAC** (attribute-based), **RBAC** (role-based), **ReBAC** (relationship-based).
- Security practices: secure cookies; preventing **CSRF**, **XSS**, and **MITM** (man-in-the-middle) attacks.
- **Audit logging** — recording login attempts, permission changes, privilege escalation, and access to sensitive data.
- **Safe error messages** — don't leak details to attackers; respond consistently across failure types; use rate limiting and account lockout.
- **Timing attacks** — checking a password involves slow hashing, so "wrong password" might take slightly longer than "unknown user". An attacker could measure that tiny difference to learn which usernames exist. It is hard to exploit, but it is still a hole worth closing.

### 3.6 Validation and transformation

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/09 Validations and Transformations/09 Validations and Transformations|09 Validations and Transformations]]

**Validation** checks that incoming data is acceptable. Three kinds:

| Kind | Question it asks | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Syntactic** | Is it in the right *shape*? | Is this a valid email / phone / date format? |
| **Semantic** | Does it make *sense*? | Date of birth can't be in the future; age is 1–120 |
| **Type** | Is it the right *type*? | Is this a string, an integer, an array, an object? |

**Client-side vs server-side validation:**

- Client-side (in the browser) gives instant feedback → better user experience.
- Server-side is the **real security** — it guards your business logic. Always do it, even if the front end already validates. Keep both sides consistent.
- **Fail fast:** reject bad input early so you don't waste work.

**Transformation** changes data into the form your code needs:

- **Type casting** — query and path parameters always arrive as strings. If you expect a numeric `id`, convert `"42"` → `42` before it reaches your handler.
- **Date formats** — convert whatever the front end sends into the format you expect (e.g. a timestamp).
- **Normalization** — make data consistent: lowercase emails, trim spaces, add a country code to phone numbers.
- **Sanitization** — clean user input to block attacks such as **SQL injection**.

**Complex validation:**

- **Relationship** — `password` must equal `confirmPassword`.
- **Conditional** — `partnerName` is only required if `married` is `true`.
- **Chained** — lowercase a string → remove special characters → check its length.

**Errors:** send clear messages the user can act on, return **all** validation errors in one response, and keep security-sensitive messages vague (say "invalid credentials", not "invalid password"). Handle failed transformations (bad JSON, unparseable dates) gracefully.

### 3.7 Middleware

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context/10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context|10 Controllers, Services, Repositories, Middlewares and Request Context]]

**Middleware** is code that runs *between* receiving a request and the final handler (or after it, on the response). Each middleware does one job and then passes control to the next one — this is **chaining**, often through a `next()` function. A middleware can also **exit early** (short-circuit), e.g. returning a 404 or 401 without reaching the handler.

**Order matters.** A typical order:

1. Log the request
2. Check authentication
3. Validate input
4. Run the route handler
5. Handle errors

Common middleware:

- **Security headers** — `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`.
- **CORS** headers, **CSRF** protection, **rate limiting**.
- **Authentication** — reuse route-protection logic everywhere.
- **Logging/monitoring** — request logs, structured logs.
- **Error handling** — turn errors into consistent API responses.
- **Compression** — shrink response bodies.
- **Body parsing** — read JSON, URL-encoded forms, and file uploads (multipart data).

Keep middleware lightweight, and remember that order affects both performance and security.

### 3.8 Request context

(Also covered in lesson 10.)

**Request context** is data attached to a single request as it flows through middleware, controllers, and services. It is **request-scoped**: it exists only while that request is being handled.

What it can hold:

- **Request metadata** — method, URL, headers, query parameters, body.
- **User/session info** — e.g. the authentication middleware looks up the user and puts them in the context, so later code can read it.
- **Tracking info** — unique request IDs or trace IDs for logs.
- **Custom data** — cached values, permission check results.

Also covered: timeouts and **cancellation signals** (stopping work when a request is abandoned). Best practices: keep it small, make sure it's cleaned up after the request (to avoid memory leaks), and don't use it as a hidden way to pass everything around.

### 3.9 Handlers, controllers, and services

(Also covered in lesson 10.)

- The **MVC pattern** (Model–View–Controller) and the responsibilities of **handlers/controllers** (deal with HTTP) vs **services** (do the actual work).
- Centralized error handling and consistent success/error response formats.
- How CRUD maps to HTTP methods:

| Operation | Method | Typical success status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create | `POST` | `201 Created` (or `400 Bad Request` if input is bad) |
| Read (list or one) | `GET` | `200 OK` |
| Update | `PUT` / `PATCH` | `200 OK` |
| Delete | `DELETE` | `200 OK` / `204 No Content` |

- **Pagination**, search, sorting, filtering.
- Best practices: strict validation, consistent responses, payload limits, hiding sensitive fields, proper auth.

### 3.10 REST API design

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/11 REST API Design/11 REST API Design|11 REST API Design]]

- **REST** — a style of API design built around **resources** (things like `users`, `orders`) and standard HTTP meaning.
- Filtering and pagination best practices.
- Versioning styles: in the URI, in a header, in the query string, or via media type.
- Designing with the **OpenAPI** spec in mind; content negotiation; meaningful error messages; client caching with ETags; handling large requests/responses.

### 3.11 Databases

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/12 Databases with Postgres/12 Databases with Postgres|12 Databases with Postgres]]

- **Relational** (tables with relationships, SQL) vs **non-relational** (NoSQL) databases, and when to use each.
- Theory: **ACID** (guarantees for transactions) and the **CAP theorem** (trade-offs in distributed systems).
- Querying and **joins**; schema design; **indexes** (speed up lookups).
- Optimization: query tuning, caching, **connection pooling** (reusing database connections).
- Data integrity: constraints, validations, **transactions**, concurrency.
- **ORMs** (Object-Relational Mappers — libraries that let you use objects instead of raw SQL): when to use one and the trade-offs.
- **Migrations** — versioned, repeatable changes to the database structure.

### 3.12 Business logic layer (BLL)

(No separate video in the playlist; related ideas appear in lesson 10.)

A request passes through three broad layers:

```
Presentation layer      → routing, middleware, validation, handlers/controllers
                           (accepts user data, sends data back)
Business logic layer    → the core rules of your app (services, domain models)
Data access layer       → talks to the database (queries, inserts, deletes)
```

The business logic layer uses the data access layer behind the scenes.

- Design principles: **separation of concerns**, **single responsibility**, **open/closed**, **dependency inversion**.
- Components: **services**, **domain models** (core things like `User`, `Order`), business rules, business validation.
- How errors should travel from the service layer up to the presentation layer.

### 3.13 Caching

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/13 Caching/13 Caching|13 Caching]]

**Caching** = keeping a copy of data somewhere faster so you don't redo expensive work. It's different from a database, which is the permanent home of the data.

- Where: in memory, browser, database; client-side vs server-side.
- **Strategies:** cache-aside, write-through, write-behind (write-back), read-through.
- **Eviction** (what to remove when full): **LRU** (least recently used), **LFU** (least frequently used), **TTL** (time to live), **FIFO** (first in, first out).
- **Invalidation** (when cached data becomes wrong): manual, TTL-based, event-based.
- **Levels:** L1 = in-memory (small, fast); L2 = network/distributed (larger, slower); **hierarchical** caching combines both — hot data in L1, less-used data in L2.
- Web caching (static assets, API responses via headers), database query caching (e.g. storing heavy join results in **Redis**), and improving the **cache hit/miss ratio**.

### 3.14 Transactional emails

(No separate video in the playlist.)

Automatic emails triggered by a user action — password resets, receipts, verification links. Anatomy: subject, preheader, header, main content, **CTA** (call-to-action button), footer, plus personalization with dynamic values like the user's name.

### 3.15 Task queues and scheduling

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs|14 Task Queues and Background Jobs]]

A **task queue** lets you hand slow work to a background worker instead of making the user wait.

- Uses: sending emails, processing images, third-party calls (payments, webhooks), heavy **batch processing**.
- **Example:** a user clicks "Delete all my data". That requires many queries across many tables. Instead of blocking the request, the server responds immediately and pushes a background job onto the queue.
- **Scheduling** (running jobs at set times): database backups, recurring reminders, data syncing, maintenance like clearing old logs or caches.
- Components: **producer** (adds tasks), **queue**, **consumer/worker** (runs tasks), **broker** (stores and delivers tasks), result **backend**.
- Task dependencies (chains, parent–child), **task groups** (run many at once and wait for all), error handling and **retries**, **prioritization** and rate limiting (e.g. payments before notifications).

### 3.16 Full-text search with Elasticsearch

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/15 Full-Text Search with Elasticsearch/15 Full-Text Search with Elasticsearch|15 Full-Text Search with Elasticsearch]]

- How it works: **inverted index** (a map from each word to the documents that contain it), **TF-IDF** (term frequency–inverse document frequency, a way to score relevance), segments, shards.
- Uses: type-ahead/autocomplete, log analytics, searching posts, profiles, comments.
- Creating and managing indexes; basic search, full-text search, relevance scoring.
- Performance: `text` vs `keyword` fields, analyzers, boosting, pagination.
- Advanced: filtering, aggregations, **fuzzy search** (tolerates typos).
- **Kibana** — a visual interface for Elasticsearch.
- Best practices: explicit field mappings, sensible number of shards, batch indexing, avoid wildcard queries.

### 3.17 Error handling

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems|16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems]]

- Error types: **syntax**, **runtime**, **logical**.
- Strategies: **fail-safe** vs **fail-fast**, **graceful degradation** (keep partial service working), prevention.
- Practices: catch early, **don't swallow errors** (ignoring them silently), custom error types, logging with **stack traces**.
- **Global error handlers**; friendly, actionable messages for users.
- Monitoring tools like **Sentry** and the **ELK stack** (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana); alerts via email or Slack.

### 3.18 Configuration management

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management|17 Configuration Management]]

Keeping settings **separate from code**, so the same code can run in different environments (development, staging, production).

- Uses: per-environment settings, safely storing **secrets** (API keys, DB passwords, certificates), **feature flags** (turn features on/off without changing code).
- Types: **static** (DB credentials, API endpoints), **dynamic** (feature flags, rate limits), **sensitive** (tokens, secrets).
- Sources: `.env` files, JSON, YAML; environment variables vs command-line flags vs static files.

### 3.19 Logging, monitoring, and observability

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability|18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability]]

- Differences between logging, tracing, monitoring, and observability.
- Log types: system, application, access, security.
- **Log levels:** `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, `FATAL`.
- **Structured** (e.g. JSON with fields) vs **unstructured** (plain text) logs.
- Best practices: centralized logging, rotation and retention, meaningful context, **never log passwords or API keys**.
- Monitoring types: infrastructure, **APM** (application performance monitoring), uptime. Tools: **Prometheus**, **Grafana**.
- Alerts: set thresholds, only alert on things someone must act on (avoid **alert fatigue**).
- **Three pillars of observability:** logs, metrics, traces. Plus security and compliance of logs.

### 3.20 Graceful shutdown

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/19 Graceful Shutdown/19 Graceful Shutdown|19 Graceful Shutdown]]

Stopping a server **without** dropping requests or corrupting data. Needed during restarts, cloud scaling, microservices, and long-running jobs.

Uses operating-system **signals** — messages sent to a running program: `SIGTERM` (please stop), `SIGINT` (interrupt, e.g. Ctrl+C), `SIGKILL` (forced stop, cannot be caught).

Steps:

1. Catch the signal.
2. Stop accepting new requests.
3. Finish requests already in progress (**in-flight**).
4. Close external resources (database connections, open files…).
5. Exit.

### 3.21 Security

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/20 Backend Security/20 Backend Security|20 Backend Security]]

- Attacks to defend against: **SQL injection**, **NoSQL injection**, **XSS**, **CSRF**, broken authentication, insecure deserialization.
- Secure design principles: **least privilege**, **defense in depth** (multiple layers of protection), **fail secure**, secure defaults, separation of duties, security by design.
- Input validation and sanitization, rate limits, **Content Security Policy**, CORS, **SameSite cookies**, monitoring security events.

### 3.22 Scaling and performance

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1|21.1 Part 1]] · [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2|21.2 Part 2]]

- Metrics: response time, resource usage; finding **bottlenecks**.
- Database: avoid the **N+1 query problem** (running one extra query per item in a list), use joins properly, **lazy loading** where appropriate, index frequently searched fields (like foreign keys).
- **Batch processing** large datasets; avoid **memory leaks** (close files and connections).
- Smaller payloads and compression to reduce network overhead.
- Performance testing and **profiling** (measuring where time is spent).
- Write clear code first — avoid **premature optimization**; keep code modular so parts can be optimized independently.
- Degrade gracefully under load; move non-critical work (emails, logging) to background queues.

### 3.23 Concurrency and parallelism

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/22 Concurrency and Parallelism/22 Concurrency and Parallelism|22 Concurrency and Parallelism]]

- **Concurrency** — handling many tasks by switching between them; helps **I/O-bound** work (waiting on network, disk, database).
- **Parallelism** — running tasks at literally the same time on multiple CPU cores; helps **CPU-bound** work (heavy calculations).

### 3.24 Object storage and large files

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/23 Object Storage Part 1/23 Object Storage Part 1|23 Part 1]] · [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/24 Object Storage Part 2/24 Object Storage Part 2|24 Part 2]]

- **Object storage** (e.g. **AWS S3**) for files like images and videos.
- Handling large files with **chunking** (splitting into pieces) and **streaming** (processing piece by piece), and **multipart uploads**.

### 3.25 Real-time backends

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/25 Real-Time Backends/25 Real-Time Backends|25 Real-Time Backends]]

- **WebSockets** (two-way live connection), **Server-Sent Events** (server pushes updates to the client), and **pub/sub** (publish/subscribe) architecture.

### 3.26 Testing and code quality

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/26 Testing for Backend Engineers/26 Testing for Backend Engineers|26 Testing for Backend Engineers]]

- Test types: unit, integration, end-to-end, functional, regression, performance, load and stress, user acceptance, security.
- **TDD** (test-driven development — write the test before the code).
- Running tests automatically in **CI/CD**; linters and formatters.
- Quality metrics:
  - **Cyclomatic complexity** — counts the number of possible paths through a function. More paths = harder to understand and test.
  - **Maintainability index** — a score for how easy code is to maintain, based on complexity, lines of code, and other factors.

### 3.27 The Twelve-Factor App

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/27 The Twelve-Factor App/27 The Twelve-Factor App|27 The Twelve-Factor App]]

A well-known set of principles for building modern, deployable web services.

### 3.28 OpenAPI

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/28 OpenAPI/28 OpenAPI|28 OpenAPI]]

**OpenAPI** is a standard format for describing an API (its paths, inputs, outputs).

- Why use it: documentation, automation (generating code, tests, clients).
- Ecosystem: **Swagger UI**, **Postman**, and other tools; history of the move from Swagger to OpenAPI; current versions (3.0, 3.1).
- Key concepts: paths, request/response definitions, parameters, schemas.
- Document structure: metadata, paths, components, security definitions, responses.
- Best practices: avoid duplication, follow the standard.
- **API-first development** — write the OpenAPI spec *before* building the API.

### 3.29 Webhooks

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/29 Webhooks/29 Webhooks|29 Webhooks]]

A **webhook** is when a server calls *your* URL to tell you something happened.

- **API polling vs webhooks:** with polling, the client keeps asking "anything new?" (client-initiated). With webhooks, the server pushes the event to you (server-initiated).
- Components: webhook URL, event triggers, payload, HTTP method, response handling.
- Best practices: **signature verification**, HTTPS, respond quickly, retries, logging.
- Testing locally with tools like **ngrok**; real examples include Stripe payments, GitHub, Slack, Discord, Twilio.

### 3.30 DevOps for backend engineers

→ [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/30 DevOps for Backend Engineers/30 DevOps for Backend Engineers|30 DevOps for Backend Engineers]]

- **CI** (continuous integration), **continuous delivery**, **continuous deployment**.
- **Infrastructure as code**, configuration management, version control.
- **Docker** (packaging apps into containers), **Kubernetes** (running and managing many containers), CI/CD pipelines.
- **Horizontal scaling** (more machines) vs **vertical scaling** (a bigger machine).
- Deployment strategies such as **blue-green** and **rolling** deployments.

---

## 4. Key takeaways

- Backend engineering is about **reliable, scalable, fault-tolerant, maintainable, efficient** systems — not just CRUD.
- Learning only through one framework creates blind spots; understanding the **underlying principles** lets your knowledge move between languages.
- The series goes roughly from **the path of a request** (HTTP, routing, serialization, auth, validation, middleware) → **data and architecture** (REST, databases, caching, queues, search) → **production concerns** (errors, config, observability, shutdown, security, scaling) → **specialized topics and delivery** (storage, real-time, testing, OpenAPI, webhooks, DevOps).

## 5. Review questions

1. Name the five qualities of good backend systems mentioned at the start. Give an example of each.
2. Why can learning backend only through one framework be a problem? Describe the Rails → Go scenario.
3. What is the difference between serialization and deserialization?
4. What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
5. Give one example each of syntactic, semantic, and type validation.
6. Why must you validate on the server even if the front end already validates?
7. Why does a numeric `id` from a URL need a transformation step?
8. Explain how a timing attack could reveal valid usernames.
9. Why does middleware order matter? Write out a sensible order.
10. What is request context, and why is it called "request-scoped"?
11. Name the three layers a request passes through and what each does.
12. What is the difference between L1 and L2 caching?
13. Why would you push "delete all my data" into a task queue instead of doing it in the request?
14. List the steps of a graceful shutdown.
15. Which helps I/O-bound work — concurrency or parallelism? Which helps CPU-bound work?
16. How do webhooks differ from polling an API?

---

## Source

- [1. Roadmap for backend from first principles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0Rwb4Xmlcwc&list=PLui3EUkuMTPgZcV0QhQrOcwMPcBCcd_Q1) — written from the video's auto-generated transcript. Some terms were mis-transcribed and have been corrected to their standard names (for example ABAC/RBAC/ReBAC, SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGKILL, ngrok, Stripe, Twilio). The deployment strategy transcribed as "red green" is written here as the standard term **blue-green**. One tool name in the OpenAPI section was unclear in the transcript and is left out.
